newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs patrol Moslem frontline villages.
newsitem.headline: Serbs patrol Moslem frontline villages.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb minister led a Serb police patrol on Wednesday through three villages within their territory but resettled by some pre-war Moslem residents.
Dragan Kijac, interior minister of the Serb republic which covers half of Bosnia, entered the village of Jusici with about 40 Serb policemen, including members of the Serb special forces.

The Serbs joined NATO peace troops and international police in joint patrols in Jusici and the nearby village of Dugi Dio in northeast Bosnia to reassert the Serbs' authority over the district and its Moslem residents.
"I would like to see the situation in Jusici, to see if you accept the laws and the constitution of the Serb republic," Kijac told the villagers.
The spokesman for the U.N.'s International Police Task Force (IPTF), Andrea Angeli, confirmed earlier reports that the Serb police had found a small arms cache in Dugi Dio village.
The patrol stopped searching the rest of the village and a third on their agenda, Mahala, after the discovery.
Angeli said Serb police confiscated the two rifles, two hand grenades, and some ammunition they found in one house, and tried to arrest the householder -- a 47-year-old Moslem.
He said after negotiations that NATO peace troops and the Serb police agreed the man would be handed to Serb authorities in nearby Zvornik at 9 a.m. (0700 GMT) on Thursday.

IPTF officials and Kijac met in Zvornik to discuss the joint patrols late on Wednesday, although a report by the Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA quoted Zvornik police chief Dragomir Vasic as saying the police patrols were over.
SRNA reported that the Moslems burned a Serb flag. It was not imediately clear if it was the same flag that the Serb police earlier raised in the centre of Dugi Dio.

About 100 Moslem men moved back last month to the three villages, which lie just inside Serb territory within the so-called "zone of separation" -- a demilitarised strip of land dividing the former warring factions.
They crossed into the deserted villages under provisions of the Dayton peace accord which guarantee freedom of movement and the right of refugees to return to their homes.
The villages lie in a sensitive region. After a tense round of negotiations, the Moslems agreed to withdraw and go through a formal registration process to confirm they were the original residents.
Most went back last Sunday under an agreement which provided for regular patrols by Serb and U.N. police.
SRNA quoted Kijac as saying the both the arms discovery and the flag-burning incident clearly demonstrated the Moslems' attitude to the Bosnian Serb Republic.
"I personally have been assured of the Moslems' hatred for the Bosnian Serb Republic, and their lack of readiness to abide by Bosnian Serb laws," he reportedly told IFOR and the IPTF.
"The Bosnian Serb government will reach its final decision and instruct the Interior ministry about how to act in the process of controlling these villages in the future," he said.
